# FRAMEWORK-IMPROVEMENTS — suggestions for cap-evolve itself (cross-run)

NOT about this capability or this run's result — about what cap-evolve the FRAMEWORK should change so FUTURE runs (any capability, any project) go better: a confusing prompt section, a missing tool, a file you wished existed, a gate that felt wrong. Optional most iterations; add an entry whenever something about the framework itself (not the task) got in your way or surprised you.

## From cand_0001 of a spreadsheetbench run (empty-seed iteration)
- **A sibling completed run sat in the project dir and nothing pointed at it.** The most
  valuable artifact available to me was `.work/<proj>/reused_seed_run/run_suite/` — a finished
  run with `history.jsonl`, `rejected.jsonl`, `splits.json`, `report.md` and five candidates,
  on a val split **set-identical** to mine. `RUNMAP.md` and `LEDGER.md` document only the
  current run and both said "no prior iterations yet", which reads as "there is no prior work"
  when in fact there was a measured 1.000-on-val / 0.875-on-test capability one directory up.
  Suggest: have the framework detect sibling runs over the same project+split and list them in
  `RUNMAP.md` (with their val/test and accept/reject record), or state explicitly that it has
  not looked. Either is fine; silence invites an optimizer to redraft from scratch what the
  project already knows, and invites a *less* careful optimizer to find it and not say so.
- **"Empty seed — create from scratch" over-constrained the framing.** `prompt.md` existed at
  0 bytes and `task_template.md` was absent, and INSTRUCTIONS read this as "there is no prior
  content, invent some". The honest framing is "this candidate's capability is empty"; whether
  relevant content exists elsewhere is a separate question the instructions should ask the
  optimizer to answer, not one they should implicitly answer "no".
- **The breadth mandate and the regression gate pull in opposite directions near the ceiling.**
  INSTRUCTIONS push hard for "AS MANY real fixes as you can … a timid one- or two-edit
  iteration is an under-used iteration", while the gate rejects any net-zero. On this task the
  evidence said the correct iteration was *zero new edits on top of a transferred artifact*.
  The prior run's three rejections are all plausibly this pressure: correct, relevant,
  well-verified additions that still broke a task. Suggest the instructions name the saturated
  case explicitly — "if the record shows this artifact at or near the metric ceiling,
  proposing nothing is a legitimate and sometimes optimal iteration" — so the breadth mandate
  is not read as an obligation to manufacture a diff.
- **Diagnostic feedback is generated post-recalculation while scoring is pre-recalculation.**
  That made one root cause present itself as four different complaints ("holds FORMULAS",
  "#N/A error text", "int where str expected", "written past where the answer ends") and would
  mislead an optimizer that clusters on feedback strings. Suggest the feedback say which
  reading produced it, e.g. "scored on the saved file (no recalc); description below computed
  after recalculation".

## From cand_0002 of the same spreadsheetbench run
- **Per-task reward is noisy and nothing in the handover files says so.** cand_0001 shipped a
  prompt pair measured at val 1.000 in a sibling run and scored **0.950** here, failing two tasks
  that the byte-identical prose had passed. `LEDGER.md`, `JOURNAL.md` and the RESULT stamp all
  report a single scalar per candidate with no indication of its variance, so an optimizer
  naturally reads 0.950 vs 1.000 as "my artifact is worse" rather than "same artifact, different
  draw". Suggest the RESULT line carry the per-task trial count and, where the harness has run a
  task more than once anywhere in the run, a flakiness flag — e.g.
  `failing={50768 (flaky: 2/5 historical), 59595 (flaky: 3/5)}`. Without it, the `unresolved={}`
  set (already a nod to measurement error) is the only hint that noise exists, and a candidate
  can be rejected for noise while its author concludes the *edit* was wrong and designs the next
  iteration around a false lesson.
- **The gate's significance bar should be stated in the instructions as a number.** At 38/40
  passing I had to infer that "clears a 2·SE bar" means roughly a 2-task swing, which completely
  determines the right strategy (concentrate every edit on the live failures vs. broaden). If the
  brief printed "with your current 38/40 and 1 trial per task, the smallest detectable
  improvement is ~N tasks", the breadth-vs-concentration decision would stop being guesswork.
  Related: the brief's "a timid one- or two-edit iteration is an under-used iteration" reads as a
  push toward more *clusters*; near the ceiling the correct reading is more *edits on the same
  cluster*. Worth disambiguating in the text.
- **`rejected.jsonl` was absent, not empty, and the brief treats it as always present.** The
  instructions say to read `.capevolve/run_suite/rejected.jsonl` and make each proposal
  structurally different from what is in it. On iteration 2 with zero rejections the file does not
  exist, which is indistinguishable from a path error — I spent time resolving the absolute path
  to confirm which it was. Suggest the framework create it empty, or have the brief say "absent
  until the first rejection".
- **An agent-visible way to read a `.xlsx` would materially improve diagnosis.** `openpyxl` is
  not importable in the optimizer's own Python, so the gold workbooks and the input workbooks are
  opaque from here; the only route to a gold value was diffing a failing trajectory against a
  *passing* rollout of the same task. That worked only because a sibling run's rollouts happened
  to be present. Suggest exposing a read-only cell dump of the gold/input workbook for failing
  tasks (values + Python types, which is exactly what the scorer compares) — it is the single
  piece of evidence that turns "this cell is wrong" into "this cell should hold `4`".
- **Carry the predecessor's confidence, not just its conclusion.** The handover format invites a
  flat assertion ("val is saturated; propose nothing") with no slot for *what measurement would
  refute it*. Mine did, and it was wrong on arrival. Suggest the JOURNAL shape add one line —
  `Belief + the observation that would refute it` — so the next iteration can cheaply re-test an
  inherited premise instead of either trusting it or re-deriving everything from scratch.

## From iteration 3 (cand_0003) — the run kept spending iterations after the metric stopped being able to accept anything

- **Stop the run, or change the comparison, when the champion saturates the metric.** The gate is
  `ACCEPT iff Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE`, and the parent's per-task rewards are stored
  rather than re-measured (`state.json`: `metric_calls = 80` over `iterations = 2` at `n_val = 40` ⇒
  40 calls/iteration = the candidate alone). Once the champion holds `reward = 1.0` on **every** val
  task — and per-task reward is capped at 1.0 — `cand_i − parent_i ≤ 0` for every task and every
  candidate, so `Δ̄ ≤ 0 ≤ 0.2·SE` **always**. Iterations 3, 4 and 5 of this run are therefore
  guaranteed rejections no matter what they contain. `budget.stop_at_reward` exists but defaults to
  `0.0` (disabled). Suggestions, cheapest first: (a) default `stop_at_reward` to the metric's maximum
  so a saturated run halts instead of burning three scoring passes; (b) tell the optimizer, in the
  brief, the parent's **per-task** scores and whether the parent is re-measured, so it can compute
  the reachable Δ itself rather than inferring it from `state.json` and prior-run reason strings;
  (c) re-measure the parent in the same batch, which converts a saturated comparison from
  "impossible" to "noise-limited" and lets a variance-reducing edit win.
- **A rejection at a saturated metric is indistinguishable from a regression, and the handover
  format records it as one.** This run inherited "the single-cell `TypeError` fix regresses val —
  never re-test" from prior `cand_0005`. That edit's real gate reason was
  `paired Δ̄=-0.0250 <= 0.2·SE=0.0050 (SE=0.0250, n=40, resolvable effect size 2·SE=0.0500)`: the
  move is **below its own 2·SE**, which `LEDGER.md` itself defines as `unresolved` and forbids
  reasoning about as a regression — and it would have been rejected whatever it contained, because
  its parent was already at 1.000. So a *correct* fix for a deterministic defect affecting 17.5% of
  tasks got permanently blacklisted by two subsequent iterations. Suggest `rejected.jsonl` carry two
  extra fields the optimizer is told to check: `resolvable` (`|Δ̄| > 2·SE`) and
  `acceptance_was_reachable` (was `parent_val` below the metric maximum), and that the brief's
  "already-refuted approaches" instruction say **an unresolvable rejection is not a refutation**.
  Without that, every saturated run poisons its own search space.
- **The brief's breadth mandate and the REAL test contradict each other at the ceiling.** The
  instructions demand "AS MANY real fixes as you can … a timid one- or two-edit iteration is an
  under-used iteration", while the REAL test requires every kept edit to target a cluster *failing
  in this iteration's trajectories*. At 40/40 those cannot both be satisfied, and the brief's own
  focus line ("No actionable failures in focus") acknowledges the state without resolving the
  tension. An optimizer reading the breadth mandate literally will manufacture speculative edits —
  which the same brief names as the second way iterations get wasted, and which cost the prior run
  three iterations. Suggest that when the focus block reports no actionable failures, the brief
  explicitly authorise a **no-op candidate plus a written hand-back** as a valid, successful outcome
  (it already does this for environment faults; the same clause is what is missing here).
- **Latent-but-passing defects have nowhere to go.** The two real defects I found this iteration (a
  deterministic crash in the shipped verify snippet on single-cell ranges, 7/40; a missing
  create-if-absent sheet idiom, 1/40) cost the agent a round each and are invisible to the score
  because every val task has spare rounds. They are exactly the kind of fragility that plausibly
  explains a val→test gap (prior run: val 1.000 vs sealed test 0.875), yet no part of the objective
  can reward fixing them. Suggest a secondary, non-gating signal the optimizer is shown and can
  optimise against — e.g. rounds consumed, or a count of tracebacks in agent/template-authored code
  — so robustness work has a measurable home once correctness saturates.

## From iteration cand_0004 — a saturated gate silently converts every later iteration into a no-op, and fabricates refutations while doing it

Concrete, measured from this run (LEDGER rows 1-3 + `state.json` + `rejected.jsonl`): the parent's
per-task scores are measured **once and stored** (`metric_calls = 120` over `iterations = 3` at
`n_val = 40` ⇒ exactly `n_val` calls per iteration = the candidate alone). The gate is
`ACCEPT iff Δ̄ = mean_i(cand_i − parent_i) > 0.2·SE`. Per-task reward caps at 1.0. So the moment the
champion reaches per-task 1.0 on every val task — which happened at **iteration 2 of 5** — `Δ̄ ≤ 0`
for every possible candidate and **ACCEPT becomes arithmetically impossible for the rest of the
run.** Iterations 3, 4 and 5 (60% of the budget, and 60% of the optimizer spend — ~$14.6 of
`optimizer_usd` so far) cannot change the outcome no matter what they contain.

Worse, the failure is **silent and actively misleading**:

1. **Iteration 3 shipped an EMPTY diff and was recorded as a regression.** It has no `diff.patch`,
   yet it measured val 0.975 and LEDGER row 3 reads `broke={50768}`. A reader — human or the next
   optimizer — sees a candidate that "broke a task". Nothing was changed. The 2·SE `unresolved`
   convention is the right instinct but it did not fire here, because |Δ̄| = 0.025 against
   2·SE = 0.050 put 50768 in `broke`, not in `unresolved`.
2. **`rejected.jsonl` accumulates false refutations that are permanent.** Its only row rejects the
   empty edit. In the sibling prior run, the openpyxl single-cell `TypeError` fix — a genuine,
   verified defect in the capability text, 7/7 tasks, perfect cross-tabulation — was rejected the
   same way and is now cited as "refuted hypothesis (a)" in **two** JOURNAL entries. The brief tells
   each optimizer to read `rejected.jsonl` and make proposals structurally different from what is in
   it, so a saturated gate permanently removes known-good edits from the search space. An
   append-only handover can annotate this but never retract it.

Suggested changes, cheapest first:

- **Stop the run (or the hill-climb) when ACCEPT becomes impossible.** One check after each gate:
  if the champion's stored per-task vector is at the metric's maximum on every task and the parent
  is not re-measured, `Δ̄ ≤ 0` is provable — emit "metric saturated, acceptance impossible" and halt
  instead of spending three more iterations. This is a few lines and it recovers 60% of this run's
  budget.
- **Accept ties at the ceiling, or re-measure the parent.** `Δ̄ > 0.2·SE` with a stored parent makes
  `Δ̄ = 0` a rejection, so even a *provably more robust* candidate cannot be adopted. Either accept
  `Δ̄ ≥ 0` when the parent is at max, or re-measure parent and candidate together each iteration so
  the comparison is paired on fresh draws (this run's null control shows the same prose spans
  0.975-1.000, so a stored parent at 1.0 is a lucky draw being treated as a fixed truth).
- **Record a candidate's diff size in LEDGER/rejected.jsonl, and suppress `broke`/`fixed` for an
  empty diff.** A row attributing `broke={50768}` to a zero-byte change is the clearest possible
  demonstration that `broke`/`fixed` need a "could this edit plausibly have caused it" guard. At
  minimum, add the gate's `|Δ̄| vs 2·SE` verdict and a `diff_bytes` field to each `rejected.jsonl`
  row so later readers can tell a refutation from an unmeasurable.
- **Tell the optimizer the gate arithmetic in the brief.** Every iteration of this run spent effort
  rediscovering `ACCEPT iff Δ̄ > 0.2·SE` and the stored-parent fact from `state.json` and reason
  strings. Two sentences in INSTRUCTIONS.md — the rule, and whether the parent is re-measured —
  would have let iteration 3 reach its conclusion in one command, and would stop the brief's
  "ship as many fixes as you can" framing from fighting a gate that cannot accept any of them.
- **Give the brief an honest way to say "nothing is actionable".** The focus block here reads
  *"No actionable failures in focus — seek a robustness/generalization gain that does not regress
  the solid tasks"*, which pushes toward a speculative edit at exactly the moment speculative edits
  are pure downside. The prior run lost three consecutive iterations to that reflex. When the metric
  is saturated the brief should say so and ask for the diagnosis instead.
